subject: Climate & Environment
title: Climate Change and Species Shifts
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Climate Change and Species Shifts.

hook.text: Species are moving toward the poles at an average of 17 kilometers per decade.

buildup.text: As temperatures rise, habitats shift. Species must migrate or adapt — or perish.

discovery.text: Mountain species climb higher. But peaks have a limit — there's nowhere left to go.

twist.text: Coral bleaching, polar bear decline, and frog extinctions are all driven by warming.

climax.text: At 2°C of warming, 18% of insect species and 8% of plants lose over half their range.

punchline.text: Species evolved for a stable climate. Stability is disappearing.

quiz.question: How fast are species moving toward the poles on average?

details.summary: Climate change is forcing species to shift their ranges poleward and upslope at an average rate of 17 kilometers per decade. Species that cannot move fast enough, like corals and mountain endemics, face extinction as suitable habitat shrinks.
details.whyItMatters: Climate-driven range shifts reshape ecosystems and create novel species combinations with unpredictable outcomes. It is the fastest-growing extinction driver this century.
takeaways: Species are shifting poleward at roughly 17 km per decade on average
Mountain species run out of higher habitat to colonize
Coral reefs face bleaching at just 1 to 2 degrees of warming

faq.question: Why can't all species simply move to cooler areas?
faq.answer: Many species depend on specific soils, food plants, or symbiotic partners that cannot move at the same pace. Physical barriers like oceans, cities, and mountain ranges block migration. Slow-reproducing species simply cannot keep pace.

faq.question: How does climate change cause coral bleaching?
faq.answer: Corals expel their symbiotic algae when water temperatures rise just 1 to 2 degrees above normal for extended periods. Without the algae, corals starve and turn white. Repeated bleaching events can kill entire reef systems.
